demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Mr. Rajiv Patel was an 80-year-old South Asian widower who had spent his career in the Coast Guard. His traumatic experience occurred decades ago when he accidentally caused a serious injury to another crew member during a rescue operation. Since then, Mr. Patel has lived with the constant shadow of this event, finding it difficult to move forward. The natural environment, particularly being near water or open spaces, triggered profound distress in him. He often avoided such settings because they reminded him of the traumatic day. The sirens from emergency vehicles would evoke a visceral response, plunging him into a state of hypervigilance and fear. The sound would trigger fragmented memories, pieces that jumbled together but never formed a coherent whole. Mr. Patel's memory of the event was sporadic; it came in disconnected snippets that were hard to recall deliberately. When these fragments surfaced, they felt vividly real, overwhelming him with intense sensory details. This pattern of memory loss and reliving made it difficult for him to talk about the future without being consumed by his past trauma. He had developed a series of maladaptive strategies to cope with his distress. He often told himself that the event did not really happen or was less severe than he knew it to be, attempting to push away the painful thoughts and force himself into a state of positivity. However, these efforts only exacerbated his fragmented memories and reinforced his negative self-appraisals. The fear of being in unfamiliar places increased as he became more certain that there was something fundamentally wrong with him-a defective core that made such incidents inevitable. This conviction led him to avoid new experiences, choosing instead the safety of familiar surroundings where he could always assess potential dangers. His hypervigilance grew, and he found himself constantly on guard, convinced that any moment could lead to another tragic event. Mr. Patel's thoughts and behaviors created a vicious cycle. The memory fragments would trigger his distress, leading him to avoid natural environments and emergency sounds. He believed that these triggers were evidence of his defective self, which in turn fueled his maladaptive strategies. When he tried to suppress the memories or force positive thoughts, it made them more difficult to recall deliberately and intensified his fragmented recollections. His hypervigilance extended into his daily life, influencing how he chose to sit, always seeking a safe position that would provide a sense of security. This constant state of alertness was both exhausting and isolating, limiting his interactions with others. He found himself avoiding conversations about the future because it only highlighted his fears. The combination of negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies had severe consequences in his life. His hypervigilance led him to take unnecessary risks as a way to confront his fears head-on, but this often resulted in increased anxiety and self-blame. The cycle seemed unbreakable; each component fed into the others, deepening his distress. Finally, it was the inability to engage with family and friends without these intrusive thoughts that brought Mr. Patel to seek help. He was most afraid of being forever trapped by his trauma, unable to find peace or move forward. What he most hoped for was a way to break free from this relentless cycle and regain some semblance of normalcy in his life.
